title: Hosea 5:8–15
context: An alarm sounds in Gibeah, Ramah, and Beth Aven, towns in the territory of Benjamin near the border between Israel and Judah (5:8). Many interpreters connect 5:8–15 with the Syro-Ephraimite conflict of the 730s BC, when Israel and Aram moved against Judah and Assyria intervened (compare 2 Kings 16:5–9; Isaiah 7:1–9); this setting is widely proposed but not certain, and the site identifications, especially Beth Aven, are held with care. Both Ephraim and Judah fall under judgment: Judah’s princes are like those who move a landmark (5:10), and the LORD is like a moth and rottenness, then like a lion (5:12, 14). When the two kingdoms saw their wounds, Ephraim turned to Assyria and sent to “King Jareb” (5:13), probably an epithet rather than a personal name, whose identity is uncertain. The LORD then withdraws “until they acknowledge their offense, and seek my face” (5:15), a line that leads into the call to return in 6:1–3. For how the LORD’s use of foreign powers fits with his justice, the site’s existing discussion at Judges 9:23 applies. Shared ground: both traditions read the passage as covenant judgment that aims at return, and both see trust in foreign powers as misplaced.

verses.text: “Blow the cornet in Gibeah, and the trumpet in Ramah! Sound a battle cry at Beth Aven, behind you, Benjamin!
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD orders alarms in Gibeah, Ramah, and Beth Aven, towns in the territory of Benjamin near the border between Israel and Judah. Arminian readers hear an urgent warning, the kind that still allows a response, and many link the scene with an invasion moving along that border.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the trumpet as the herald of the LORD’s judgment, whose timing he controls. Shared ground: both traditions note that many interpreters connect 5:8–15 with the Syro-Ephraimite conflict (compare 2 Kings 16:5–9; Isaiah 7:1–9), a setting widely proposed but not certain, and both treat the site identifications, including Beth Aven, with care.

verses.text: Ephraim will become a desolation in the day of rebuke. Among the tribes of Israel, I have made known that which will surely be.
verses.arminianNotes: “Ephraim will become a desolation in the day of rebuke.” Arminian readers stress that the LORD announced this beforehand among the tribes; the warning itself is a mercy, giving opportunity to heed the word before the day arrives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize “that which will surely be”: the LORD declares the certainty of his judgment and makes his purpose known in advance. Shared ground: both traditions affirm that God’s announced judgment is sure and that his warning also summons the hearers, and both read the advance announcement as a sign that the LORD acts openly and justly.

verses.text: The princes of Judah are like those who remove a landmark. I will pour out my wrath on them like water.
verses.arminianNotes: “The princes of Judah are like those who remove a landmark.” Moving boundary stones was a covenant crime (compare Deuteronomy 19:14; 27:17). Arminian readers see Judah’s leaders exploiting a crisis for gain, and some read the charge as seizure of border territory during the conflict, though this is uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the LORD’s wrath poured out “like water” as abundant, overwhelming judgment on leaders who violate the covenant’s protections for property and inheritance. Shared ground: both traditions read the image as covenant violation by Judah’s rulers, hold literal and figurative readings of the landmark cautiously, and see the LORD as defender of what he apportioned.

verses.text: Ephraim is oppressed, he is crushed in judgment, because he is intent in his pursuit of idols.
verses.arminianNotes: “Ephraim is oppressed, he is crushed in judgment, because he is intent in his pursuit of idols.” Arminian readers note the causal link: oppression follows from a chosen and persistent pursuit, and the suffering is the bitter fruit of a course Ephraim set for himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s judgment at work in Ephraim’s oppression, whether through foreign powers or internal turmoil, and see the intent on idols as the settled direction of the heart. Shared ground: both traditions read the oppression as judgment connected to idolatry, and both see the LORD as the one who governs these events in history.

verses.text: Therefore I am to Ephraim like a moth, and to the house of Judah like rottenness.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore I am to Ephraim like a moth, and to the house of Judah like rottenness.” The images are of slow, quiet decay rather than sudden destruction. Arminian readers see the gradual process as giving time to recognize the decline and turn before it is complete.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the startling first person: the LORD himself is the hidden cause of the decay, working within the nation before any outward collapse. Shared ground: both traditions read the moth and the rot as images of gradual decline sent by the LORD, and both note the contrast with the sudden lion of verse 14.

verses.text: “When Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah his wound, then Ephraim went to Assyria, and sent to King Jareb: but he is not able to heal you, neither will he cure you of your wound.
verses.arminianNotes: When Ephraim and Judah saw their sickness and wound, “Ephraim went to Assyria, and sent to King Jareb.” Arminian readers see the tragedy of turning to human powers for healing instead of to the LORD, a free choice of misplaced trust that cannot deliver what it promises.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the verdict “he is not able to heal you”: no earthly power can cure what God has inflicted. Shared ground: both traditions note that “King Jareb” is probably an epithet rather than a personal name, perhaps meaning a contending or great king, and that its identity, often linked with an Assyrian ruler, is uncertain (compare 2 Kings 15:19–20; 17:3–4).

verses.text: For I will be to Ephraim like a lion, and like a young lion to the house of Judah. I myself will tear in pieces and go away. I will carry off, and there will be no one to deliver.
verses.arminianNotes: “For I will be to Ephraim like a lion, and like a young lion to the house of Judah.” Arminian readers stress that the lion is the same LORD whose care was refused, and that “there will be no one to deliver” exposes the futility of the alliance sought in verse 13.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the emphatic “I myself will tear in pieces”: whatever nation serves as the instrument, the LORD is the agent of judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the image as covenant judgment, see foreign armies as instruments under God’s rule, and note that the one who tears is the one who heals in 6:1.

verses.text: I will go and return to my place, until they acknowledge their offense, and seek my face. In their affliction they will seek me earnestly.”
verses.arminianNotes: “I will go and return to my place, until they acknowledge their offense, and seek my face.” Arminian readers see the withdrawal as purposeful: the LORD waits for genuine acknowledgment, and the closing words, “In their affliction they will seek me earnestly,” express hope that suffering will awaken repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the “until” as revealing God’s purpose to bring his people back, so that the affliction he sends becomes the means by which he produces earnest seeking. Shared ground: both traditions read the withdrawal as remedial; on how repentance relates to God’s response, see the existing discussion at Judges 10:16, which treats a similar return.
